title: Pendo Without the Tagging Mess
intro: Pendo usually ends up as a messaging tool or a pile of tags nobody trusts. The fix is strategy before tags.

learn.title: Why “tag everything” fails
learn.text:
**Auto-tagging tracks layout, not intent.** In big custom apps it produces vague names like div1 or buttonX that flow into funnels and dashboards and look like tracking.

**Every tag is an assumption.** One Submit button tagged three ways (submitButton_v1, btn-submit-primary, untagged) made one product show a 20% drop-off and another none, because of set-up, not UX.

Calabro's rule: assume all tagging is manual.

try.q: Product A shows a 20% drop-off on Submit; product B shows none. What should you check first?
options: Whether the same button is tagged the same way
Whether product B's form design is simply clearer
Whether product A has many more active users
Whether the two date ranges differ by a week
try.explain: Inconsistent tags create differences that look like UX problems.

learn.title: Start with strategy
learn.text:
**Executives:** What user behaviour do you need to see? Which metrics are already reported across business units, and which are missing?

**Product teams:** Where do users get stuck? How do people move through complex workflows? Where does behaviour differ from what you expected?

ResearchOps turns the gap into **one shared tagging plan**, so teams don't each invent their own and fragment the data.

try.q: Who do you talk to first, before any tagging?
options: Executives, then product teams
Developers first, then the designers
Customer support, then the sales team
Users first, then the analytics vendor
try.explain: Leaders define what must be visible; teams say where users struggle.

learn.title: Top tasks: 10–15
learn.text:
**1.** List the common tasks: roughly the 20% of actions that make up 80% of use.
**2.** Add rare but high-impact ones (exporting an audit log matters for trust and compliance).
**3.** Trim to **10–15 core tasks**: merge similar ones, keep the most representative, favour tasks that take different paths.

Those tasks decide what gets tagged.

try.q: Exporting an audit log is used rarely. Should it be a top task?
options: Yes, if it matters for trust or compliance
No, top tasks are the most frequent only
Only if a customer asks for it
Only after the first quarter of data
try.explain: Rare but high-impact tasks belong on the list.

learn.title: Funnels: 3–6 steps, feature tags
learn.text:
A funnel has a **start trigger** (Create report), meaningful **midpoints**, and a **completion trigger** (Submit, Save, Done). 1–2 steps give too little data; 7+ get noisy.

**Feature tags** → use: clear intent, precise timestamps.
**Page tags** → mostly avoid: they over-count on refreshes and idle time. OK as a static confirmation exit step.
**Track events** → sparingly: accurate but cost developer time.
**Guides** → never in funnels: they can simulate interactions.

try.q: Why are page tags weak funnel steps?
options: They fire passively and over-count
They need extra developer time to set up
They can't record precise timestamps at all
They only work on the mobile version
try.explain: Refreshes and idle time inflate page counts.

learn.title: Then dashboards, guides, paths
learn.text:
**Pull, not push:** give leaders a dashboard of meaningful funnels — completion rate, drop-off points, time on task, adoption, comparisons across releases — and their questions create the teams' interest. Pair it with one standard survey everywhere (SUS, SUPR-Q or NPS).

**Guides last:** treat each one as a UX project, and keep interruptions very rare.

**Paths and Journeys** are for exploring once the baseline is reliable.

try.q: When should in-app guides roll out widely?
options: After top tasks are tagged and funnels exist
On day one, to drive adoption as fast as possible
Only after Paths and Journeys are fully set up
Whenever any product team requests one for a feature
try.explain: Overlapping guides hurt usability and skew the data.

test.q: What does Calabro recommend about auto-tagging in a large custom app?
options: Assume all tagging is manual
Use it, then rename the vague tags later
Use it, but only for the page-level tags
Use it during the first month, then stop
test.explain: Auto-tags reflect layout, not intent, and break in custom components.

test.q: How many core tasks should drive the first tagging plan?
options: About 10 to 15, covering common and critical tasks
Every action available in the product
Only the top three features by usage
Around 50, roughly one per screen
test.explain: Narrow common plus rare-but-critical tasks to 10–15.

options: Create report → add data → Submit, on feature tags
Nine steps that cover every optional branch of the flow
Two page views: the dashboard, then the settings page
A welcome guide, then the home page, then any click
test.explain: 3–6 steps, a clear start and finish, feature tags, no guides.

test.q: What are Paths and Journeys for?
options: Exploring once a reliable baseline exists
Replacing funnels in the executive reporting
Triggering in-app guides at the right moment
Counting page views per session across apps
test.explain: Funnels first for benchmarks; Paths and Journeys to explore later.

test.q: How do you get product teams to use the data?
options: Give leaders a funnel dashboard so they ask
Send a weekly analytics report to every team
Require every team to tag its own features
Add a guide asking users for their feedback
test.explain: Pull, not push: leaders' questions create demand.
